newsitem.title: USA: Japan trade figures push dollar to lower US debut.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade figures push dollar to lower US debut.

text.p: The dollar stood broadly lower at the U.S. open, hurt by a sharp rise in Japan's preliminary June trade surplus and profit-taking in sterling/mark.

Japan's Finance Ministry reported on Monday that the country's trade surplus rose 129.3 percent on a year-over-year basis in the first 20 days of June and suggested that the full monthly figure would also rise for the third consecutive month.
The data pushed dollar/yen to a low of 111.98 and filtered through to dollar weakness against other major currencies as well.

"We saw a big move in dollar/yen earlier and more recently the downward move in sterling," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics. "The market was a little long late last week and due for a correction."

The dollar began at 112.30/35 yen and 1.7455/58 marks. At the close of trading on Thursday, ahead of the long Independence Day holiday in the U.S., the dollar had been quoted at 113.77/87 yen and 1.7530/40 marks.
Dealers said it had made further progress in overseas trading on Friday.
The British pound fell against the dollar and the mark following a surprise 1.1 percent decline in May manufacturing output -- the largest drop since June 1993.
Analysts, who had been expecting a small increase of 0.2 percent, blamed the decrease on recent sterling strength.
In the wake of the number, market observers were still calling for an interest rate hike from the Bank of England later this week. However, prospects for a 50 basis point rise appeared slim.

"The weakish number in the UK led to some overdue consolidation in cable after a huge runup following the budget speech last week," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co.
"People are most definitely still banking on a rate hike but if (the Bank of England) surprises and does nothing ... we will see a mad rush for the exit doors."
Cable was quoted at $1.6840/50 in opening trade, down from Thursday's closing rate of $1.6910/20. The pound also slipped to a low of 2.9320 marks in overseas trade, after an earlier peak of 2.9625.
In addition to dollar and sterling profit-taking, the mark also garnered support from more acerbic euro-related comments from Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber.

Stoiber, who has frustrated German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in recent weeks with his staunch opposition to a flexible interpretation of Maastricht criteria for monetary union, was quoted in the Monday edition of the Financial Times as saying that a "controlled delay" in the launching of the single currency would be better than a weak euro.
Dealers said the dollar's ability to hold above 1.7420 marks was encouraging. They pegged key support in dollar/yen between 111.80 and 112, where knock-out options are rumored to be lurking.
"The markets are a little jittery but still technically sound against Europe," said Strauss. "Against the yen, the key levels are well known."

In other news on Monday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the Group of 10 would continue to monitor foreign exchange market developments closely, but refused to make further comments on recent dollar strength.
News that the European Union had given qualified approval to Italy's EMU economic plans had little impact on mark/lira.
The dollar opened at 1.4578/83 Swiss francs, down from Thursday's closing rate of 1.4687/97, and at Canadian $1.3719/24, down from C$1.3733/38. The Australian dollar debuted at $0.7428/33.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
